claim: By 2050, as many as 10 million people may die annually from antimicrobial-resistant infections.
source: By 2050, as many as 10 million people may die annually from antimicrobial-resistant infections (WHO, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2019 report

claim: Phage therapy uses viruses (phage) that infect pathogenic bacteria to clear infections.
source: Phage therapy uses viruses (phage) that infect pathogenic bacteria to clear infections (Kwiatek et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwiatek et al., 2020

claim: Phage therapy is species-specific and does not harm beneficial microbiota.
source: Phage therapy has several advantages to antibiotics by being species-specific (thus not harming beneficial microbiota) (Koskella and Meaden, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Koskella and Meaden, 2013

claim: Phages are self-amplifying at infection sites.
source: Phage therapy has several advantages to antibiotics by being species-specific (thus not harming beneficial microbiota) (Koskella and Meaden, 2013) and self-amplifying at infection sites (Górski et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Górski et al., 2015

claim: Bacteria can evolve resistance to phages within hours.
source: A major consideration with the use of therapeutic phages is the ease and speed (sometimes within hours) at which bacteria can evolve resistance, which can greatly limit the therapeutic potential of phages (Jariah and Hakim, 2019; Torres-Barceló, 2018; Torres-Barceló and Hochberg, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jariah and Hakim, 2019; Torres-Barceló, 2018; Torres-Barceló and Hochberg, 2016

claim: Phage can sometimes evolve to overcome bacterial resistance.
source: First, phage can sometimes evolve to overcome this resistance (i.e., bacteria-phage coevolution) and so they may continue lowering bacterial densities (Gandon et al., 2008; Hampton et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gandon et al., 2008; Hampton et al., 2020

claim: Phage resistance can trade-off against bacterial growth rates and virulence.
source: Second, resistance can trade-off against bacterial growth rates and virulence; as the alteration or loss of bacterial surface structures, typically associated with phage resistance, can affect other fitness-related phenotypes such as nutrient uptake, biofilm formation, and binding of host receptors (Mangalea and Duerkop, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mangalea and Duerkop, 2020

claim: The nasal cavity can act as a source of infection from highly drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus when patients undergo hospitalization and are treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics.
source: The nasal cavity can act as a source of infection, notably from highly drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus when patients undergo hospitalization and are treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics (Mainz et al., 2009; Wertheim et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mainz et al., 2009; Wertheim et al., 2004

claim: Of the 24 ancestral isolates isolated in vivo at day 0, 23 were susceptible to both the ancestral phage (14–1 and PNM) while one was resistant to 14–1 but susceptible to PNM.
source: Of the 24 ancestral isolates isolated in vivo at day 0, 23 were susceptible to both the ancestral phage (14–1 and PNM) while one was resistant to 14–1 but susceptible to PNM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from resistance testing of ancestral isolates

claim: All ancestral bacteria were susceptible to phage isolated from the patient during and after decolonization.
source: All ancestral bacteria were susceptible to phage isolated from the patient during and after decolonization (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: After 2 days of in vivo phage therapy, more than half of bacterial isolates were resistant to ancestral phage.
source: After 2 days, we saw evidence of resistance evolution, with more than half of bacterial isolates being resistant to ancestral phage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from time-shift assays

claim: One of the two isolates isolated at day 4 was phage resistant and no P. aeruginosa was detected from nasal swabs after this time point.
source: One of the two isolates isolated at day 4 was phage resistant and no P. aeruginosa was detected from nasal swabs after this time point.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bacterial isolation and resistance testing

claim: Bacterial populations from days 2 and 4 showed observationally higher phage resistance (87.5% day 2, 100% day 4) against day 2 phage, but this was nonsignificantly different to resistance shown to ancestral phage and phage from days 4 and 7.
source: Although both bacterial populations from days 2 and 4 showed observationally higher phage resistance (87.5% day 2, 100% day 4) against day 2 phage, this was nonsignificantly different to resistance shown to ancestral phage and phage from days 4 and 7 (Tukey HSD: p>0.05; Supplementary file 1; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Tukey HSD) of experimental data shown in Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1

claim: Resistance to phage increased through time in vitro, reaching comparable levels to that observed in vivo (>50%).
source: Resistance to phage increased through time, reaching comparable levels to that observed in vivo (>50%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in vitro evolution experiments

claim: There was a significantly higher proportion of bacteria resistant to contemporary phage at the end of the experiment in the treatment where phages were added once (90.81%) compared to when phages were added repeatedly (66.7%).
source: there was a significantly higher proportion of bacteria resistant to contemporary phage present at the end of the experiment in the treatment where phages were added once (90.81%, ±SE=0.0003) compared to when phages were added repeatedly (66.7%, ±SE=7.64; Tukey HSD comparing phage added once and repeatedly, treatments:estimate=–1.63, z-ratio=–3.75, p=0.0002; Figure 1b, c).
evidence: Supported by Tukey HSD statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1b and c

claim: All isolates from the control condition were susceptible to ancestral phages.
source: All isolates from the control condition were susceptible to ancestral phages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from resistance testing

claim: When phages were added once, resistance to ancestral phage (14–1: 88.64%; PNM: 90.15%) did not differ relative to phage isolated at the end of experimental evolution (90.0%).
source: When phages were added once, resistance to ancestral phage (14–1: 88.64%, ±SE=2.77; PNM: 90.15%, ±SE=2.60) did not differ relative to phage isolated at the end of experimental evolution (90.0%, ±SE=4.27); Tukey HSD comparing end-point phage resistance to contemporary phage to resistance to 14–1 (p=1.0) and PNM (p=0.938; Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by Tukey HSD statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: When phages were added repeatedly, resistance to ancestral phage (14–1: 94.41%; PNM: 96.5%) was significantly higher than to phage isolated at the end of experiment (61.5%), indicative of increased phage infectivity.
source: However, when phages were added repeatedly, resistance to ancestral phage (14–1: 94.41%, ±SE=1.93; PNM: 96.5%, ±SE=1.54) was significantly higher than to phage isolated at the end of experiment (61.5%, ±SE=12.5), indicative of increased phage infectivity (Tukey HSD comparing end-point phage resistance to contemporary phage to resistance to 14–1 (p<0.001) and PNM (p<0.001); Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by Tukey HSD statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1c

claim: The increase in phage infectivity evolved before the first sampling time point (the second transfer, or 96 hr) in the repeated phage treatment.
source: This suggests the increase in phage infectivity evolved before the first sampling time point (the second transfer, or 96 hr).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that phage resistance was independent of phage time point during experimental evolution

claim: In vivo, phage therapy reduced bacterial virulence by 95.5% on average (median hazard ratio=0.045, 95% confidence interval=0.012–0.163).
source: In vivo, phage therapy reduced bacterial virulence by 95.5% on average (median hazard ratio [HR]=0.045, 95% confidence interval [CI]=0.012–0.163).

claim: Bacteria in the phage added repeatedly treatment were 89.8% less virulent on average compared to the no-phage control populations (median HR=0.102, 95% CI=0.0294–0.355).

evidence: Supported by Bayesian regression analysis of Galleria mellonella survival data shown in Figure 2b

claim: In the control populations, 96 (80%) of the G. mellonella died within 47 hr, with death occurring at a mean time of 19 hr.

claim: In the phage added repeatedly treatment, 41.2% of G. mellonella died with a mean time to death of 35.4 hr.
